params.question: A patient presents with a punched-out ulcer covered by a thick, adherent crust on the leg. Which pyoderma does this lesion pattern indicate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Non-bullous impetigo presents as honey-coloured crusted erosions on the skin surface, typically around the mouth and nose in children — not as a punched-out ulcer.

Correct. Ecthyma is a deeper ulcerative pyoderma that presents as a punched-out ulcer beneath a thick, adherent crust, typically on the legs. Unlike superficial impetigo, it extends into the dermis and heals with scarring.
Folliculitis presents as small pustules each centred on a hair follicle. It is superficial and self-limiting, not ulcerative.
Erysipelas presents as a sharply-demarcated, raised, red, hot plaque — usually on the face or leg — not as a punched-out ulcer with a crust.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the depth-and-lesion mapping: a punched-out ulcer with an adherent crust on the leg points to ecthyma, a deeper infection that extends beyond the epidermis and heals with scarring.
Well done. Recognising the punched-out ulcer with an adherent crust as ecthyma demonstrates your grasp of the depth-and-lesion classification.

interactions.label: Which clinical situation most clearly justifies obtaining a wound swab for cultu

params.question: Which clinical situation most clearly justifies obtaining a wound swab for culture and sensitivity in a patient with pyoderma?

answers.text: A child with three honey-crusted lesions around the mouth that are responding well to topical mupirocin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is localised non-bullous impetigo already responding to first-line therapy. Culture is unnecessary when the diagnosis is clear and treatment is working.

answers.text: A young woman with a single follicular pustule on the forearm that resolved spontaneously in two days

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A self-limiting follicular pustule needs neither antibiotics nor culture. Ordering investigations for trivial, self-resolving lesions adds cost without changing management.

answers.text: A patient with recurrent furunculosis who has failed to improve after a full course of appropriate first-line antibiotics

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Both recurrence and failure of appropriate first-line therapy are key triggers for culture and sensitivity testing. This combination raises the likelihood of a resistant organism such as MRSA, and culture results will guide targeted therapy.

answers.text: An elderly man with an annular, scaly plaque showing central clearing on the forearm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This description is classic for tinea (a dermatophyte fungal infection), not pyoderma. The appropriate investigation here is a KOH preparation for fungal hyphae, not a bacterial culture.

overallFeedback.feedback: The video identifies three triggers for culture: recurrence, failure of appropriate first-line therapy, and suspicion of resistant organisms such as MRSA. When none of these is present, empirical treatment suffices.
Excellent. You correctly identified a situation where culture will change management — recurrent infection failing first-line therapy suggests a resistant organism.

interactions.label: Mupirocin retains activity against many MRSA strains because its mechanism of ac

params.question: Mupirocin retains activity against many MRSA strains because its mechanism of action differs from beta-lactam antibiotics. Which mechanism does mupirocin use?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cell wall synthesis inhibition is the mechanism of beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins). MRSA is resistant precisely because it has an altered cell wall target. Mupirocin works by an entirely different pathway.

Correct. Mupirocin blocks isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase, an enzyme essential for bacterial protein synthesis. Because this target is unrelated to the penicillin-binding proteins that MRSA has altered, mupirocin retains activity against many MRSA strains.
DNA gyrase inhibition is the mechanism of fluoroquinolones (e.g. ciprofloxacin), not mupirocin.
Folic acid synthesis inhibition is the mechanism of sulfonamides and trimethoprim, not mupirocin.

overallFeedback.feedback: Mupirocin inhibits isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase — a unique target unrelated to cell wall synthesis. This is why it retains activity against MRSA, whose resistance is specific to beta-lactam binding.
Well done. Understanding mupirocin's unique mechanism explains both its anti-MRSA activity and why resistance to it is emerging independently of beta-lactam resistance.

interactions.label: A patient with cellulitis of the leg reports severe pain that seems far worse th

params.question: A patient with cellulitis of the leg reports severe pain that seems far worse than the modest visible redness would explain. What should this clinical finding prompt?

answers.text: Reassurance and stronger analgesia, as pain perception varies between patients

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Disproportionate pain in the context of a skin infection is not simply a variation in pain perception. It is a recognised red flag for necrotising soft-tissue infection, which demands action, not reassurance.

answers.text: Urgent surgical referral for suspected necrotising soft-tissue infection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Pain out of proportion to the visible skin findings is one of the earliest warning signs of necrotising infection, often appearing well before tissue necrosis becomes visible. Early surgical consultation at this stage saves limbs and lives.

answers.text: A Doppler ultrasound to exclude deep vein thrombosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While DVT can cause leg pain, the clinical context here is an established skin infection with disproportionate pain — a classic early sign of necrotising infection that requires surgical assessment, not a vascular workup.

answers.text: Switching from oral to intravenous antibiotics and reassessing in 24 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Escalating antibiotics and waiting is dangerous when necrotising infection is possible. Necrotising fasciitis progresses faster than antibiotics can control — surgical debridement is the definitive treatment, and delay worsens outcomes.

overallFeedback.feedback: Pain out of proportion to visible skin changes in a patient with cellulitis is a red flag for necrotising soft-tissue infection. This sign appears early, before tissue necrosis, and should prompt immediate surgical consultation — not a wait-and-see approach.
Excellent. Recognising disproportionate pain as an early harbinger of necrotising infection — before the skin shows necrosis — is the critical clinical skill for timely surgical referral.

interactions.label: When recurrent furunculosis fails to respond to an adequate course of cloxacilli

params.question: When recurrent furunculosis fails to respond to an adequate course of cloxacillin, the clinician should suspect methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and arrange culture and sensitivity testing before changing therapy.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true. Cloxacillin targets Staphylococcus aureus through cell wall synthesis; treatment failure in recurrent furunculosis should raise suspicion of MRSA. Culture and sensitivity testing at this point guides rational drug selection and avoids the trap of empirically cycling antibiotics without knowing the organism's resistance profile.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Cloxacillin is an anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam; failure to respond raises the possibility of MRSA, which has altered penicillin-binding proteins. Culture with sensitivity testing — including a D-zone test before relying on clindamycin — is essential to guide targeted therapy rather than empirically cycling drugs.
